games.title: Principles of Medical Microbiology and Parasitology: quick quiz
games.topic: Principles of Medical Microbiology and Parasitology
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 2 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which of the following bacterial structures is primarily responsible for conferring resistance to phagocytosis and plays a major role in determining virulence?
questions.explanation: The bacterial capsule is a gelatinous outer layer that inhibits phagocytosis by host immune cells, significantly enhancing virulence.

questions.q: A gram-positive bacillus that forms spores and produces a toxin complex consisting of protective antigen, lethal factor, and edematous factor is:
questions.explanation: Bacillus anthracis is a spore-forming gram-positive rod whose virulence relies on a tripartite exotoxin.

questions.q: Which laboratory diagnostic test is considered the gold standard for identifying the specific species of dermatophytes causing a tinea infection?
options: Sabouraud dextrose agar culture with microscopic examination
questions.explanation: Culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar followed by microscopic visualization of macroconidia and microconidia is the definitive method for dermatophyte species identification.

questions.q: Which mechanism of horizontal gene transfer involves the uptake of naked, extracellular DNA fragments from the surrounding environment by competent bacteria?
questions.explanation: Transformation is the genetic alteration of a cell resulting from the direct uptake and incorporation of exogenous genetic material from its surroundings.

questions.q: Which of the following parasites is transmitted through the ingestion of undercooked pork containing encysted larvae and causes periorbital edema, muscle pain, and eosinophilia?
questions.explanation: Trichinella spiralis infection occurs by eating raw or undercooked pork, leading to larval migration into striated muscle causing myalgias and marked eosinophilia.

questions.q: Beta-lactam antibiotics, such as penicillins, exert their bactericidal effect by targeting which of the following bacterial structures?
questions.explanation: Beta-lactams bind to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), inhibiting the transpeptidation reaction necessary for peptidoglycan synthesis.

questions.q: Which virus is characterized by a segmented negative-sense RNA genome and undergoes antigenic shift leading to major influenza pandemics?
questions.explanation: Influenza viruses possess segmented RNA genomes that allow for genetic reassortment (antigenic shift), resulting in novel strains capable of causing pandemics.

questions.q: A patient presents with bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). Which strain of Escherichia coli is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC), particularly serotype O157:H7, produces Shiga-like toxins that can damage endothelial cells in the renal glomeruli, leading to HUS.

questions.q: Which protozoan parasite is typically transmitted via contaminated water and causes foul-smelling, fatty diarrhea (steatorrhea) with characteristic trophozoites displaying a 'face-like' appearance?
questions.explanation: Giardia lamblia trophozoites have a characteristic bilateral symmetry resembling a face and cause malabsorptive steatorrhea.

questions.q: Which diagnostic medium is specifically selective and differential for the isolation of Vibrio cholerae from stool samples?
questions.explanation: TCBS agar is formulated specifically to select for and differentiate sucrose-fermenting Vibrio species, such as Vibrio cholerae.

games.title: Thalassemia syndromes: quick quiz
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 24-year-old Southeast Asian man is found to have microcytic anemia on routine pre-employment screening. His hemoglobin electrophoresis is normal. Genetic testing reveals deletion of two alpha-globin genes (--/aa). What is the classic clinical designation for this genotype?
questions.explanation: Deletion of two alpha-globin genes (--/aa or -a/-a) results in alpha-thalassemia trait, characterized by mild microcytic hypochromic anemia with normal adult hemoglobin electrophoresis.

questions.q: A 15-year-old patient with beta-thalassemia major who receives regular blood transfusions presents with progressive shortness of breath and lower extremity edema. Which of the following is the leading cause of mortality in patients with transfusional iron overload?
questions.explanation: Cardiac toxicity, leading to cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias due to myocardial iron deposition, remains the leading cause of death in patients with transfusion-dependent thalassemia.

questions.q: A 30-year-old asymptomatic woman of Mediterranean descent undergoes routine pre-conception screening. Complete blood count shows Hb 10.5 g/dL, MCV 64 fL, and elevated RBC count. Which hemoglobin electrophoresis finding is most characteristic of beta-thalassemia minor?
questions.explanation: Beta-thalassemia trait/minor classically presents with mild microcytic anemia and a diagnostic elevation of HbA2 (>3.5%) on hemoglobin electrophoresis.

questions.q: A 19-year-old male with beta-thalassemia major receives chronic iron chelation therapy with deferoxamine. Which of the following adverse effects requires baseline and regular periodic screening during treatment with this agent?
questions.explanation: Deferoxamine therapy requires regular audiological and ophthalmological monitoring due to risks of sensorineural ototoxicity and retinal toxicity.

questions.q: In Hemoglobin H (Hb H) disease, which molecular structure forms the characteristic unstable hemoglobin tetramers detected on brilliant cresyl blue staining?
questions.explanation: Hb H disease results from the deletion of three alpha-globin genes, leading to an excess of unpaired beta-chains that aggregate into unstable beta-4 tetramers.

questions.q: A fetus with a four-gene deletion alpha-thalassemia (--/--) develops severe fetal hydrops and intrauterine demise. Which abnormal hemoglobin predominantly accumulates in this condition?
questions.explanation: Complete absence of alpha-globin production (--/--) leads to accumulation of unpaired gamma-chains that form gamma-4 tetramers known as Hb Bart, which cannot deliver oxygen to fetal tissues.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with isolated microcytosis (MCV 62 fL) and an RBC count of 6.1 x 10^12/L. The calculated Mentzer Index (MCV / RBC count) is 10.1. This value strongly points toward which of the following diagnoses?
questions.explanation: A Mentzer Index (MCV divided by RBC count in millions/mcL) less than 13 strongly suggests thalassemia trait, whereas a ratio greater than 13 suggests iron deficiency anemia.

questions.q: Characteristic skeletal deformities such as 'chipmunk facies' and a 'hair-on-end' appearance on skull X-rays in undertreated beta-thalassemia major are caused by which underlying pathophysiological mechanism?
options: Severe intramedullary expansion of erythroid progenitor cells
Pathologic bone deposition of excess non-transferrin bound iron
Secondary hyperparathyroidism secondary to chronic renal failure
questions.explanation: Severe ineffective erythropoiesis drives massive expansion of the bone marrow within cortical bones, leading to skeletal deformities such as maxillary hypertrophy and skull diploic expansion.

questions.q: Luspatercept is an approved disease-modifying therapy for adults with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia. What is its mechanism of action?
options: Direct oral chelation of intracellular cardiac iron
Reactivation of the gamma-globin gene promoter
Erythroid maturation agent that neutralizes TGF-beta superfamily ligands
Targeted gene editing of the HBB promoter region
questions.explanation: Luspatercept functions as a recombinant fusion protein that binds SELECT TGF-beta superfamily ligands to inhibit aberrant SMAD2/3 signaling and promote late-stage erythroid maturation.

questions.q: A peripheral blood smear from a patient with untreated beta-thalassemia major shows marked anisopoikilocytosis with numerous target cells. What mechanism leads to target cell formation in thalassemia?
options: Excess erythrocyte membrane relative to reduced intracellular hemoglobin content
Intracellular precipitation of oxidized Hb H inclusion bodies
Persistent retention of residual ribosomal RNA in circulating reticulocytes
Autoimmune antibody deposition on red blood cell membrane proteins
questions.explanation: Target cells form due to a relative excess of red blood cell membrane surface area relative to its reduced intracellular hemoglobin content.

games.title: Bone & Soft Tissue Pathology: Cases, Tumors, & Answers: case showdown
games.topic: Bone & Soft Tissue Pathology: Cases, Tumors, & Answers
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 3 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 16-year-old male presents with a 3-month history of worsening left knee pain and swelling. Plain radiographs of the distal femur reveal a destructive, mixed lytic and blastic intramedullary mass with a 'sunburst' periosteal reaction and Codman triangle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Osteosarcoma typically occurs in adolescents around the knee and presents with a sunburst periosteal reaction and Codman triangle on imaging.

questions.q: An 11-year-old boy presents with localized pain and swelling in the mid-diaphysis of the right femur, accompanied by low-grade fever and leukocytosis. Radiographs show a lytic diaphyseal lesion with an 'onion-skin' periosteal reaction. Which of the following translocation markers is most characteristic of this tumor?
questions.explanation: Ewing sarcoma is characterized by the EWSR1-FLI1 gene fusion resulting from the t(11;22) translocation and classically shows an onion-skin periosteal reaction.

questions.q: A 25-year-old female presents with persistent pain around her right knee. Radiographs of the proximal tibia demonstrate a classic eccentric, radiolucent, 'soap-bubble' lytic lesion extending to the subchondral bone without a sclerotic rim. What is the most appropriate next step in management or diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Giant cell tumor of bone is a locally aggressive benign lesion typically treated with intralesional curettage and local adjuvants such as cementation or phenol.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with a deep, painless, slowly enlarging soft-tissue mass in his right thigh measuring 12 cm. Biopsy reveals mature adipocytes with significant variation in cell size, nuclear atypia, and scattered hyperchromatic stromal cells. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Well-differentiated liposarcoma (atypical lipomatous tumor) is characterized by mature fat with atypical, enlarged cells containing hyperchromatic nuclei.

questions.q: A 14-year-old male complains of severe nocturnal right tibial pain that is remarkably relieved by the administration of aspirin or ibuprofen. A small radiolucent nidus surrounded by a zone of reactive cortical sclerosis is seen on CT scan. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Osteoid osteomas characteristically present with night pain relieved by NSAIDs and feature a small radiolucent nidus with marked surrounding sclerosis.

questions.q: A 22-year-old female presents with a deep-seated, painful mass near her right knee joint, present for several months. Histological examination of the resected biphasic tumor shows a proliferation of uniform spindle cells admixed with epithelial cells forming glandular structures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Synovial sarcoma classically exhibits a biphasic histology with both epithelial and spindle cell components, despite typically arising near joints rather than from the synovium.

questions.q: A 65-year-old male with a history of long-standing Paget disease of bone presents with severe, unrelenting skull and pelvic pain and a rapidly expanding mass. Radiographs show mixed lytic and blastic bone destruction with cortical breakthrough. Malignant transformation to which tumor has most likely occurred?
questions.explanation: Paget disease carries a well-known risk of secondary malignant degeneration, most commonly into high-grade osteosarcoma.

questions.q: A 70-year-old male presents with generalized bone pain, fatigue, and recurrent infections. Laboratory workup reveals normocytic anemia, hypercalcemia, and renal insufficiency, along with a monoclonal serum IgG spike and Bence-Jones proteins in the urine. What finding would bone marrow biopsy most likely show?
options: Sheets of atypical clonal plasma cells
questions.explanation: The clinical and laboratory findings are diagnostic of multiple myeloma, which is characterized by the clonal proliferation of malignant plasma cells in the bone marrow.

games.title: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease: Hydatidiform Mole and: case showdown
games.topic: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease: Hydatidiform Mole and
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 24-year-old woman presents at 10 weeks of amenorrhea with dark brown vaginal bleeding and severe hyperemesis gravidarum. Physical examination reveals a uterus size equivalent to a 14-week gestation, and transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates a heterogenous, 'snowstorm' intrauterine mass with absent fetal tissue. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Complete hydatidiform mole typically presents with dark brown vaginal bleeding, hyperemesis, uterine size greater than expected for gestational age, and a classic 'snowstorm' ultrasound appearance without a fetus.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman undergoes suction curettage for a suspected molar pregnancy. Histopathology of the evacuated tissue reveals focal trophoblastic proliferation, marked villous hydrops admixed with normal villi, and fetal red blood cells within fetal vessels. Which karyotype is most commonly associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: Partial hydatidiform moles usually contain fetal tissue or membranes and typically possess a triploid karyotype (69,XXX, 69,XXY, or 69,XZY) resulting from dispermic fertilization of a normal egg.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman is diagnosed with a complete hydatidiform mole at 11 weeks of gestation based on serum hCG levels >100,000 mIU/mL and characteristic ultrasound findings. She is hemodynamically stable and strongly desires future fertility. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: Suction curettage is the standard initial treatment for evacuation of a hydatidiform mole to preserve fertility and minimize the risk of uterine perforation.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman undergoes successful suction evacuation of a complete hydatidiform mole. Her serum quantitative beta-hCG levels are monitored weekly until undetectable. What advice regarding contraception should be provided during the post-evacuation monitoring period?
options: Use reliable contraception for at least 6 months
No contraception is needed as fertility is temporarily impaired
Pregnancy is safe as soon as one normal menses occurs
questions.explanation: Reliable contraception is recommended during post-molar surveillance to prevent pregnancy, which would confound the interpretation of serial serum beta-hCG levels.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with hemoptysis and dyspnea 4 months following an uncomplicated term vaginal delivery. Chest radiography demonstrates multiple bilateral pulmonary nodular lesions, and her serum beta-hCG is 85,000 mIU/mL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Choriocarcinoma can develop after any pregnancy type, including normal term deliveries, and frequently metastasizes hematogenously to the lungs, presenting with respiratory symptoms and highly elevated beta-hCG.

questions.q: A 26-year-old woman who underwent evacuation of a complete mole 8 weeks ago is found to have serum beta-hCG levels that have plateaued over 3 consecutive weeks. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates a hypervascular myometrial mass. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: Post-molar gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN), diagnosed by plateauing or rising beta-hCG levels, is primarily managed with systemic chemotherapy based on risk stratification.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with irregular vaginal bleeding 1 year after an uncomplicated delivery. Histopathology of an endometrial biopsy demonstrates intermediate trophoblasts infiltrating the myometrium, with serum beta-hCG levels mildly elevated at 400 mIU/mL and markedly elevated human placental lactogen (hPL). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Placental site trophoblastic tumor arises from intermediate trophoblasts, produces low levels of beta-hCG but high human placental lactogen, and is relatively resistant to standard chemotherapy.

questions.q: A 29-year-old woman at 12 weeks gestation presents with severe nausea, palpitations, and heat intolerance. Pelvic examination reveals bilateral, markedly enlarged, multiloculated ovarian cysts (8 cm each), and serum beta-hCG is >200,000 mIU/mL. What is the primary underlying cause of these ovarian cysts?
options: Hyperstimulation of the ovaries by extremely high beta-hCG levels
Excessive progesterone secretion from the placenta
questions.explanation: Theca lutein cysts are benign, bilateral ovarian enlargements caused by hyperstimulation from excessively high circulating beta-hCG levels in molar pregnancies.
